title: The real fight in agentic commerce isn't autonomy. It's authorization
excerpt: The conversation about AI and shopping is happening in the wrong place
content_html:
The conversation about AI and shopping is happening in the wrong place.

Everyone wants to know whether agents will browse for us, compare prices for us and, eventually, buy for us without asking. It's a fair question. But it’s not the one that matters right now.

The more consequential shift is happening somewhere far less visible: inside payment networks, authorization protocols and the systems that decide whether software is allowed to spend money on our behalf.

The technical capability for an AI agent to complete a purchase has existed for some time. What has been missing is the infrastructure that allows businesses and consumers to trust those transactions: confirming an agent had permission to act, ensuring it stayed within agreed boundaries, and creating a verifiable record if something goes wrong.

Founder and Chief Innovation Officer at commercetools.

Over the past few months, that infrastructure has started to emerge. The biggest moves in this space haven't come from AI labs building increasingly showy assistants. They've come from the companies that move money.

At its annual conference, for example, Stripe used the opportunity to introduce wallets that agents can spend from, alongside a partnership letting businesses sell directly inside AI search and chat environments.

Visa introduced an early protocol to help merchants tell a legitimate AI agent apart from a bot. Mastercard announced its own framework for registering and authenticating agents before a transaction is allowed to proceed. Agents are already showing up at volume. What's been missing is the infrastructure to handle what happens next.

The limitation was never autonomy. It was authorization.

Adobe research from early this year shows that AI traffic to US retail sites grew 393% YoY in the first quarter, with AI-referred visitors converting 42% better than non-AI traffic. Just a year before, that same traffic was converting 38% below standard channels.

That’s why the language from the payments industry has shifted so noticeably toward authorization, intent and trust. Mastercard's own leadership has made things explicit: how do you distinguish a legitimate agent from a malicious one? How do you confirm the consumer really authorized the purchase? How do you verify that the agent did what it was told?

Those aren't AI questions. They're identity and trust questions that just happen to involve AI.

Whoever defines the boundary captures the value

What's notable about the recent announcements is how consistent the underlying logic is across companies that otherwise compete directly. Visa's protocol and Mastercard's framework work the same way in principle: register the agent, verify intent and pass credentials only once trust is established.

Stripe's approach, issuing single-use payment credentials per task rather than exposing a customer's card details to an agent, solves the same problem from a different angle.

The protocols may look like back-office plumbing. Functionally, they're architecture for autonomous commerce. Every time a payments provider decides what counts as a verified agent, what data has to be passed to prove intent or how disputes get resolved, it's writing rules that shape who gets to participate and on what terms.

A consumer can be persuaded by an AI assistant to want something, but if the transaction can only execute through a specific track, with specific verification steps, then influence over the purchase decision and control over the purchase itself become two separate things. The company that captures the second captures the economics, regardless of who captured the first.

For merchants, this creates a concrete operational problem. If a transaction gets disputed, can the business prove what was authorized, by whom and under what constraints? These are the exact questions Visa, Mastercard and Stripe are quickly trying to answer; whoever answers them first effectively writes the rulebook everyone else follows.

The race that's already started

Autonomous shopping is imminent, and in some categories it’ll come faster than in others. Routine reordering and B2B procurement are likely to happen first. Other more considered, emotionally fueled purchases will take longer; trust has to be earned. Payment readiness is only part of it, however.

The commerce stack underneath, covering product data, pricing, inventory and checkout, needs to be structured and accessible enough for agents to actually operate it. Businesses that haven't addressed that layer will find the payments question is the least of their problems.

The infrastructure being built right now by payment providers won't just process agent-driven transactions. It will determine which businesses are visible to agents in the first place, which transactions are trusted by default and which get pushed into friction and manual review. The real battle isn’t over autonomy. It’s over who owns the infrastructure of trust.

content_html_zh:
关于人工智能和购物的讨论发生在错误的地方。

每个人都想知道代理商是否会为我们浏览、为我们比较价格，并最终在不询问的情况下为我们购买。 这是一个公平的问题。 但这不是现在最重要的。

更重要的转变正在一些不太明显的地方发生：支付网络内部、授权协议以及决定软件是否被允许代表我们花钱的系统。

人工智能代理完成购买的技术能力已经存在一段时间了。 所缺少的是允许企业和消费者信任这些交易的基础设施：确认代理有权采取行动，确保其保持在商定的范围内，并在出现问题时创建可验证的记录。

commercetools 的创始人兼首席创新官。

在过去的几个月里，该基础设施已经开始出现。 这个领域最大的举措并不是来自人工智能实验室打造的越来越引人注目的助手。 他们来自转移资金的公司。

例如，在其年度会议上，Stripe 利用这个机会介绍了代理商可以使用的钱包，以及允许企业直接在人工智能搜索和聊天环境中进行销售的合作伙伴关系。

Visa 推出了一项早期协议，帮助商家区分合法的人工智能代理和机器人。 万事达卡宣布了自己的框架，用于在允许交易进行之前注册和验证代理。 代理商已经大量出现。 所缺少的是处理接下来发生的事情的基础设施。

限制从来都不是自治。 这是授权。

Adobe 今年年初的研究显示，第一季度美国零售网站的 AI 流量同比增长 393%，AI 推荐的访客转化率比非 AI 流量高 42%。 就在一年前，同样的流量转化率比标准渠道低 38%。

这就是为什么支付行业的语言如此明显地转向授权、意图和信任。 万事达卡自己的领导层已经明确了这一点：如何区分合法代理人和恶意代理人？ 如何确认消费者确实授权购买？ 您如何验证代理人是否按照指示行事？

这些不是人工智能问题。 它们是恰好涉及人工智能的身份和信任问题。

谁定义了边界，谁就捕获了价值

最近的公告值得注意的是，在其他直接竞争的公司之间，基本逻辑是多么一致。 Visa 的协议和 Mastercard 的框架原则上以相同的方式工作：仅在建立信任后才注册代理、验证意图并传递凭证。

Stripe 的方法是根据任务发放一次性支付凭证，而不是将客户的卡详细信息暴露给代理，从不同的角度解决了同样的问题。

这些协议可能看起来像后台管道。 从功能上讲，它们是自主商业的架构。 每当支付提供商决定什么算作经过验证的代理、必须传递哪些数据来证明意图或如何解决争议时，它都会制定规则来决定谁可以参与以及以什么条件参与。

消费者可以被人工智能助手说服想要某种东西，但如果交易只能通过特定的轨道、特定的验证步骤来执行，那么对购买决策的影响和对购买本身的控制就变成了两件事。 抓住第二个机会的公司就抓住了经济机会，不管谁抓住了第一个机会。

对于商家来说，这造成了具体的运营问题。 如果交易出现争议，企业能否证明授权内容、授权人以及限制条件？ 这些正是 Visa、Mastercard 和 Stripe 正在迅速尝试回答的问题；谁先回答这些问题，谁就有效地编写了其他人都遵循的规则手册。

比赛已经开始

自主购物迫在眉睫，并且在某些类别中它会比其他类别来得更快。 例行重新订购和 B2B 采购可能会首先发生。 其他更经过深思熟虑、情绪化的购买将需要更长的时间；必须赢得信任。 然而，支付准备只是其中的一部分。

底层的商务堆栈涵盖产品数据、定价、库存和结账，需要足够的结构化和可访问性，以便代理商能够实际操作它。 尚未解决该问题的企业会发现支付问题只是他们面临的最不重要的问题。

支付提供商目前正在构建的基础设施不仅仅处理代理驱动的交易。 它将首先确定哪些业务对代理可见，哪些交易默认受信任，哪些交易会陷入摩擦和人工审查。 真正的战斗不是围绕自治。 问题在于谁拥有信任基础设施。
